title: time() function in C - GeeksforGeeks
content:
The time() function is a standard library function defined in the <time.h> header file in C and <ctime> in C++. It returns the current calendar time as the number of seconds elapsed since 00:00:00 UTC, January 1, 1970 (Unix Epoch).

  • Returns the current time as a Unix timestamp in seconds.
  • Can also store the returned time in a user-provided time_t object if a valid pointer is passed.
C 
#include <stdio.h>
#include <time.h>

int main ()
{
    time_t seconds;
    
    seconds = time(NULL);
    printf("Seconds since January 1, 1970 = %ld\n", seconds);
    
    return(0);
}

Output
Seconds since January 1, 1970 = 1538123990

Syntax  

time_t time( time_t *second )

Parameter: This function accepts single parameter second. This parameter is used to set the time_t object which store the time.
Return Value: This function returns current calendar time as a object of type time_t.

Advantages

The time() function provides a simple and portable way to obtain the current system time for various time-related operations.

  • Returns the current calendar time as a Unix timestamp in seconds.
  • Can directly store the current time in a time_t object through the function parameter.
  • Widely supported across C and C++ compilers, making it portable.

Limitations

Although time() is useful for obtaining the current time, it has some limitations.

  • Returns time only in seconds, so it cannot measure milliseconds or microseconds.
  • Depends on the system clock, so incorrect system time affects the returned value.
  • Suitable for general timekeeping but not for high-precision performance measurements.
